messages.subject: CFA using lavaan in R with RStudio vs FACTOR
messages.subject_clean: CFA using lavaan in R with RStudio vs FACTOR
messages.body_plain:
Hello:
   I'm not a programmer, a statistician nor a marh wizard but a social worker accustomed to using SPSSPC & formerly SPSSX. So I've been informed that the version of SPPPC I have does not do Confirmatory Factor Analysis and was recommended R with lavaan as a way of getting the CFA results I need. What I have done so far?
1) Downloaded R (multiple authorizations required in our system--initially in VINCI but more readily handled at the local PC)
2) Installed RStudio
3) Downloaded lavaan
4) Oriented on how to upload data into R and did so.
5) Seen tutorials in YouTube for CFA and found them very technical for a beginner
6) Meanwhile was recommended to use FACTOR and do a Hull analysis with a Oblique Procrustean rotation on my data---did so with the remote guidance of the packages creator...found my data has one factor and not three as in study hypothesis. Was told by a psychometrician that was all I needed to go ahead and write it up.

My study: Adaptation of an 18 item scale with three dimensions (6 items each) from English  to Spanish. Hypothesis is that we would find same three dimensions in Spanish as in the English version. Items are Likert from 1 to 5 with 100 subjects. Exploratory Factor Analysis gave us three factors using the 1.000 eigenvalue criteria but the scree test showed a steep slope after 1st factor and leveling off after that with a relatively small proportion of the variance explained by the other factors. We got stalled in the study upon realizing our siftware did not have CFA and we have been struggling with that threafter.

Question is, as this is all very technical would it help any if I continue my venture into R and proceed with the lavaan analysis or would that be a waste of time ( I still would need step by step guidance on how to run it).

Jaime Alvelo
San Juan, Puerto Rico

messages.subject: semTools update
messages.subject_clean: semTools update
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

We have updated semTools to version 0.4-5. It is available on our repository. You may access it by typing the following line in your R console:

install.packages("semTools", repos="http://rweb.quant.ku.edu/kran", type="source")

Note that this version of semTools is not available on CRAN because we are using hidden functions in lavaan. When this issue is fixed, we will update it on CRAN.

Here are the details for this update:

The measurementInvarianceCat function is available for automatically implementing measurement invariance for categorical indicators. ThepartialInvariance and partialInvarianceCat functions are also available to easily find partial invariance models. Click here <https://github.com/simsem/semTools/wiki/Partial-Measurement-Invariance> for the detailed explanation of how these functions work. ThesingleParamTest function is added to run a post-hoc analysis after nested model comparison to find the constraint (with 1 df) that makes nested models different. The SSpower function is added to implement the power analysis using Satorra and Bentler's (1985) method. The averaged variance extracted (AVE) is available in the reliability function. The fixed factor method of scale identification is available in the measurementInvariance function by specifying std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE.

Please let me know if you have any questions, problems, or comments.

Best,
Sunthud

messages.subject: Re: formative measurement model for CFA
messages.subject_clean: formative measurement model for CFA
messages.body_plain:
> I am wondering if I have to add in my model the correlations between the formative indicators of one factor. For example of factor Z, the correlations between  Y1, Y2,  Y3, Y4, v60_R , Y6 ,Y7. Or should I wait for the modification indices and their values?
>

 I don't think you need to specify them explicitly, those correlations should be included default.  But I don't think your model will run because your formative constructs are not identified.  A formative construct has no definition unless it predicts something else, either by having additional reflective indicators or by being a predictor of other constructs that are themselves identified.  Your construct Z is only an outcome, but is not observed, so it is not identified.  Because Z is not identified, I don't think Y3, Y4, Y6, or Y7 are identified either, since they don't predict anything (except Z, which is not identified).

Terry

Anyway thanks for the recommendation
Jaime

messages.subject_clean: runMI for lavaan::sem: Subscript out of bounds
messages.body_plain:
Dear experts,

I hope that you can help me with an error-report when I run runMI. I post here because I noticed another user a year ago reported something similar (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/lavaan/j1mfUaofxRQ/B_Z4_W5tarAJ).

This command: runMI(cid.sem.only, data = mice.imp, fun = "sem", estimator = "WLSMV")
generates this error: Error in `[<-`(`*tmp*`, rhs, lhs, value = 1) : subscript out of bounds

The relevant part of the script looks like this:

------------------------ SCRIPT BEGINS ------------------------
library(mice)
library(lavaan)
library(semTools)

# Create dataset for analysis on imputed data
mice.imp <- NULL
m=5
for(i in 1:m){
mice.imp[[i]] <- complete(data.imp,action=i,include=FALSE)
}

## SEM Model
cid.sem.only<-'
    citA =~ cit1 + cit4
    cceA =~ cce1 + cce4
    ciaA =~ cia2 + cia3
    oitA =~ oit1 + oit2 + oit3 + oit4
    oceA =~ oce1 + oce2 + oce3 + oce4
    oiaA =~ oia1 + oia2 + oia3 + oia4
    witA =~ wit1 + wit2 + wit3 + wit4
    wceA =~ wce1 + wce2 + wce3 + wce4
    wiaA =~ wia1 + wia2 + wia3 + wia4

    cid =~ citA + cceA + ciaA
    oid =~ oitA + oceA + oiaA
    wid =~ witA + wceA + wiaA

    cid ~ oid + wid
    oid ~ wid
'
cid.only.fit<- runMI(cid.sem.only, data = mice.imp, fun = "sem", estimator = "WLSMV")

------------------------ SCRIPT ENDS ------------------------

The multiply imputed dataset has been created with the MICE-package. Analysis for the complete datasets (m = 5) works fine.
I tried following the instructions from the link to the post similar to this one but either it does not work or I am doing something wrong (which is most likely).

Could I kindly ask for your help with getting the above model to work?

If I left something out or you need additional information please let me know and I will provide it.

Best regards,
Mikkel G. Hangaard

PhD. student at
Department for Language and Communication
University of Southern Denmark

messages.body_plain:
Dear Terry,
Dear other lavaan users,

Is it nog enough to determine the missing Y's in the Z part of the syntax by the following part of the syntax:

Y1  =~ v71 + v72

Y2 =~v4801 + v4802 + v4803 + v4804 + v4805 + v4806 + v4807 + v4809

Y3 <~X1 + X2 + v50_R + v51_R + v40_R

X1 =~ v3503 + v3509 + v3510

X2 =~v3504 + v3507 + v3508

Y4 <~ v61_R + v62_R

Y6 <~v80_R + v26_R + v27_R + X3

X3 =~ v3201 + v3202 + v3203 + v3204 + v3205 + v3206 + v3207 + v3208Y

Y7 <~v90_R + v91_R

Here are some reflective scales and for every Y there are manifest variables?

Thank you all for your help,

Kind regards,

Sofie Van Regenmrotel

2014-08-05 6:32 GMT+02:00 Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com>:

>
> > I am wondering if I have to add in my model the correlations between the formative indicators of one factor. For example of factor Z, the correlations between  Y1, Y2,  Y3, Y4, v60_R , Y6 ,Y7. Or should I wait for the modification indices and their values?
> >
>  I don't think you need to specify them explicitly, those correlations should be included default.  But I don't think your model will run because your formative constructs are not identified.  A formative construct has no definition unless it predicts something else, either by having additional reflective indicators or by being a predictor of other constructs that are themselves identified.  Your construct Z is only an outcome, but is not observed, so it is not identified.  Because Z is not identified, I don't think Y3, Y4, Y6, or Y7 are identified either, since they don't predict anything (except Z, which is not identified).
>
> Terry

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

Following the good advice given to me in this thread https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/lavaan/R1K2KKINygI I managed to get my sem-models to work.

However, it seems version 0.4-5 has brought with it another problem. One of my CFA models that used to work in 0.4 now produce this error:

     1. Convergence 2. Proper SE 3. Proper Variance Estimate Used for pooling
[1,]           TRUE         TRUE                       FALSE            FALSE
[2,]           TRUE         TRUE                       FALSE            FALSE
[3,]           TRUE         TRUE                        TRUE             TRUE
[4,]           TRUE         TRUE                       FALSE            FALSE
[5,]           TRUE         TRUE                       FALSE            FALSE
Error in runMI(cfa.oid.model4, data = mice.imp, fun = "cfa", std.lv <http://std.lv> = F,  :
  Please increase the number of imputations. The number of convergent replications is less than or equal to 1. See the details above.

The script looks like this:
cfa.oid.model4<-'

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mikkel,

I'm not sure I would quantify this as a "bug" in either version, it is more of a philosophical switch. This error only occurs when either 0 or 1 of the imputed data sets produce a model that converges. When 0 of the models converge there are not results to view so the error makes sense. With 1 model converged there are "results" (which were reported in earlier versions) but they aren't the results from multiple imputation. Instead they are based on a single imputation (so no pooling needs to be done). runMI provides you with the imputed data set that did converge (in your case #3) so if you wanted to see the results from that data set you could use the cfa command in lavaan on only that imputed data set. I wouldn't recommend drawing too many conclusions from a single imputation (hence the warning) but it might be useful to diagnose specific issues with the model (especially in this case where it seems like the other imputed data sets are giving you improper estimates of variances).

Alex

Seongo:
       The author of the original scale in English  already had done a EFA on a large data sample and found three factors. He then reduced an initial 50 item scale with three of the factors to an 18 item scale (taking an equal amount of items for each of the factors. Our team using a bicultural team approach and cross-cultural methods adapted the the scale to Spanish (forward & bacward translation using professional translators & testing for comprehension). What we wanted to to was to verify that in the Spanish version were an equivalent number of factors as in the original English version (original has copyright and we had permission from author).
Our idea was to use CFA to test whether we had the same factors and the items fell equally into each factor. We had a dated software version of SPSS that did not do CFA with no funds to buy the expensive software so we began to expore available shareware. We came to find R with the lavaan option and our psychometrician reccommende the FACTOR program. In FACTOR we did the following:

messages.subject_clean: CFA using lavaan in R with RStudio vs FACTOR
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jaime,

Okay, I got it. You want to make a Spanish item scale, right?

First, FACTOR can Exploratory Factor Analysis, not CFA. So, Procrustes rotation criteria is not a CFA method. That's just a kind of EFA method.

Second, You can use another estimator in lavaan when you try CFA. It may help fitting your data in your model.

Like this:

> HS.model <- '
> burden  =~ V1 + V2 + V10 + V16 + V17 + V18
> sadness =~ V4 + V8 + V9 + V11 + V12 + V15

> worry   =~ V3 + V5 + V6 + V7 + V13 + V14
> '
>
> fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, estimator='WLSMV', ordered=names(HolzingerSwineford1939))
> summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)

Third, Please do not use the Eigenvalue greater than one rule (as known as Kaiser rules) when you try to estimate EFA models. That's not accurate criteria. You can try to calculate CFI, TLI and RMSEA when you estimate the EFA model via fa() in psych(), efaUnrotate() in semTools(), and mirt() with the M2 statistic. CFI and TLI > .9 and RMSEA Upper < .08 are may useful to find factor structure of Spanish Scale.

If you feel that's too hard to execute, I can help you freely.
You can ask privately via my e-mail with Developmental sample for EFA and Validation Sample for CFA.

--
Seongho Bae
seo...@kw.ac.kr

Master of Psychology in Industrial & Organizational Psychology.

messages.body_plain:
Here is the Scale validation process:

1. Split half of file randomly. One is for doing EFA what will call 'Developmental Sample', the other is doing CFA what will call 'Validation Sample'.
2. In EFA, Increasing factors with checking the model fit based on chi-square (CFI, TLI, RMSEA), Communality, etc. with Developmental sample.
3. In CFA, Check the EFA model is right using an EFA structure with Validation sample.

messages.body_plain:
> I just read, that lavaan can handle a LV with a single indicator. Can I specify the residual variance of the single indicator? (Since I already got that from the Rasch-Model...

Yes, if you have a factor "F" defined by a single indicator "x", the sem() and cfa() functions automatically fix the residual variance to zero, but you can specify the error variance (e.g., as 0.34) of an observed variable as the variable's covariance with itself:

modelsyntax <- '
F =~ x
x ~~ 0.34*x
'

Set the argument std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE or FALSE to control whether you freely estimate the factor loading or factor variance, fixing the other to 1.

Terry

Hi All,

I am very new to Lavaan, R and statistics generally.

I successfully used Lavaan to run a SEM analysis on my data, that's where the romance ends. Interpreting the data has been a challenge. I will be grateful if i can get some direction.

OGAR

=====================================================
Questions
=====================================================
.To what extent does System quality affect user satisfaction and benefits in e-Learning systems?
• To what extent does system quality affect user satisfaction in e-Learning systems?
• To what extent does information quality affect user satisfaction in e-Learning systems?
• To what extent does instructional quality affect user satisfaction in e-Learning systems?
• To what extent does user satisfaction affect the benefits of the e-Learning system?
======================================================================
variables
===========================================================
SYQ : System Quality
IFQ : Information Quality
ISQ: Instructional Quality
USR: User Satisfaction
BEN: Benefits

=========================================
Lavaan Code
==========================================

#Latent variables

SYQ=~syq1+syq2+syq3
IFQ=~ifq1+ifq2+ifq3
ISQ=~isq1+isq2+isq3
USR=~us1+us2+us3
BEN=~be1+be2+be3

#Regression Model
USR~SYQ+IFQ+ISQ
BEN~USR
'

Pdata<-read.csv("SEM_Data_Thesis.csv")
 Pfit<-cfa(CMS,data=Pdata)
 summary(Pfit, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)
 lavaan.diagram(Pfit, title = "Perception Model Diagram")

semPaths(Pfit, intercepts = FALSE)

Thanks, sure, but the Rasch-model gives me a variance for every case. Is there a chance to specify this column in the model?

Am Samstag, 9. August 2014 05:32:24 UTC+2 schrieb Terrence Jorgensen:
>
> > I just read, that lavaan can handle a LV with a single indicator. Can I specify the residual variance of the single indicator? (Since I already got that from the Rasch-Model...
>
> Yes, if you have a factor "F" defined by a single indicator "x", the sem() and cfa() functions automatically fix the residual variance to zero, but you can specify the error variance (e.g., as 0.34) of an observed variable as the variable's covariance with itself:
>
> modelsyntax <- '
> F =~ x
> x ~~ 0.34*x
> '
>
> Set the argument std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE or FALSE to control whether you freely estimate the factor loading or factor variance, fixing the other to 1.
>
> Terry

messages.body_plain:
Dear Yves,

Related to our conversation about WLSMV(S) estimator for categorical data, and to an error message mentioned by Ulrich Schroeders, I have the following two questions:

1. When I used lavaan 0.5-14 and dev 0.5-15 a year ago, I obtained convergence for a model using WLSMVS estimator and missing="pairwise", while today, using the same data and the same options when fitting the model, with version 0.5-16, the model does not converge.

I have looked through the version history on the lavaan project website, but not been able to find an explanation there.
(The bugs mentioned for 0.5-15 concerning the polychoric correlation between two variables and missing="pairwise" (if data are categorical) do not seem to apply because I use 0.5-16, and moreover don't have binary variables, nor do I have exogenous covariates as I am running a CFA model).

Has anything in the algorithms behind WLSMVS changed that might explain the divergent results?

When I looked again into the results of the converged model using the old lavaan vesion, I noticed that some fit indices were almost too good to be true: CFI = 1, TLI = 1.018, RMSEA = 0.000 90% ConfInt RMSEA = [0.000, 0.000] - not sure whether this information helps you.

2. When I specify my model slightly differently, I also see a new error messages which never appeared in the same analysis with the previous versions:
Error in if (fx < 0) fx <- 0 : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
In addition: Warning message: In lav_samplestats_from_data(lavdata = lavdata, missing = lavoptions$missing, : lavaan WARNING: number of observations (427) too small to compute Gamma

Ulrich in his post in this thread on 7/27/2013 mentioned the first error as well (but not the second) and you might have found the reason for the error message he mentioned  but no further answer is visible on the forum thread.

In advance many thanks for your help,
Franziska

messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan-users,

I am experiencing very long computation times. Running 'sem' is really slow with my model and (probably out of ignorance) I am unable to figure out why. Perhaps I have to many parameters?

For convenience I have attached one of the imputed datasets for the variables in question (n = 796).

The model looks like this:

-------------- SCRIPT BEGINS --------------
cid.sem.only<-'
    cit =~ cit1 + cit4
    cce =~ cce1 + cce4
    cia =~ cia2 + cia3
    oit =~ oit1 + oit2 + oit3 + oit4
    oce =~ oce1 + oce2 + oce3 + oce4
    oia =~ oia1 + oia2 + oia3 + oia4
    wit =~ wit1 + wit2 + wit3 + wit4
    wce =~ wce1 + wce2 + wce3 + wce4
    wia =~ wia1 + wia2 + wia3 + wia4
    pit =~ pit1 + pit2 + pit3 + pit4
    pce =~ pce1 + pce2 + pce3 + pce4
    pia =~ pia1 + pia2 + pia3 + pia4

    cid =~ cit + cce + cia
    oid =~ oit + oce + oia
    wid =~ wit + wce + wia
    pid =~ pit + pce + pia

    cid ~ oid + wid + pid
    oid ~ wid
    wid ~ pid
'

test.sem <- sem(cid.sem.only, data = test.data, estimator = "WLSMV")

-------------- SCRIPT ENDS --------------

I can have the computer run for hours with no result. Is this to be expected?

Thanks for any help you may provide.

Best regards,
Mikkel

messages.subject: RE: Question on computation time
messages.subject_clean: Question on computation time
messages.body_plain:
Mikkel—

     You are specifying a second order factor model.  The sem function automatically scales the first level factors by fixing the first loading to 1, but I do not believe the sem function automatically scales the second order factors (cid, oid, wid, pid).  These factors also need scaling, and uncertainty about this might be causing an identification problem, which could make an algorithm cycle for a long time.  You may be able to remove this problem by specifying scale for those four factors.  You might do this by explicitly fixing one loading to 1, just as you do with the first order indicators, i.e.:

    cid =~ 1*cit + cce + cia

--Ed Rigdon

Oh, sorry.

If you cannot collect more samples, that is may okay. The CFA result is okay. High correlation and the sample size problem are just a limitation.

Seongho Bae.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jaime

I dont agree with the recomendation that you got about the neccesary sample size. Acording to these rules it would be impossible to have enough sample to estimate complex models, I have work models with more than 200 parameters.

The way you define the neccesary sample size would be with a proper power analysis. A power analysis for CFA is basically a small simulation with varying sample sizes. In R you can do this with the simsem package ( https://github.com/simsem/simsem/blob/master/SupportingDocs/Examples/Version05/ex18/ex18.R ), in this link you can see an example of a power analysis.

Remember that for CFA what is analyzed is the covariance matrix, not the individual data, so, if your sample is a good representation (on the covariance matrix) of the population you are good with a relatively small sample.

I think that N=100 should be enough to estimate a model with 3 factors CFA. If the measures have good quality 100 its usually enough

Hope this helps, and gives more hope.

Bye

--- Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your input Mauricio. Sample size estimation would have had to be done prior to the study so that Seongho has pointed out to a limitation that must be acknowledged if you we are to publish in refereed journals where experts review your submitted article. We based our items on an already established scale in the English language done with a rigorous methodology and a good size sample. We used and inter-disciplinary approach using cross-cultural methodology for the adapatation of the instrument to our language. But as the instrument had clinical applications to its sub-scale scores we could not proceed to accepting just the rigorous forward and backward translation method. We proceeded to a field test replicating the original study and finding equivalent already validated scales to test for construct validity of the translated scale. We found that culture impacted the dimensions of the construct and thus we will not be recommending the use of the sub-scales. Nonetheless the full 18 item scale is still usable for clinical purposes and we will publish its use in the near future. I have two PhD psychologists with vast experience in my team who who will help me with the technical pieces of psychometrics. We do want to appreciate the observations & recommendations of :
Jeremy Miles
Terence Jorgensen
Seongo Bae
Mauricio Garnier

It is these supports that motivates us to continue research even if unfunded.
Jaime Alvelo, DSW
San Juan, Puerto Rico

messages.subject: Issue with composite variable
messages.subject_clean: Issue with composite variable
messages.body_plain:
Dear  lavaan users,

apologies for the total beginner's question. I am trying to create a composite variable and I have done it successfully, but I am bit confused about how to fix the scale. I am attaching some data with a few lines of codes, to show what puzzles me. Please bear in mind that this is just an example and my composite will have many more variables! What I do not understand is the parameter estimate for my composite. In its non-composite version it is negative and then it becomes positive on one occasion.

# read data set
dat<-read.csv("newdf.csv")

# no composite
no.compo<-'F~T'
standardizedSolution(sem(no.compo,data=dat))

#1) fix scale of composite using parameter estimate from model without composite

compo1<-'lat<~-0.061*T
          F~lat'
standardizedSolution(sem(compo1,data=dat))

#2) fix scale of composite fixing path of baseline indicator to 1

compo2<-'lat<~1*T
          F~lat'
standardizedSolution(sem(compo2,data=dat))

#3) fix scale of composite using parameter estimate from model without composite (using absolute value of parameter estimate)
compo3<-'lat<~0.061*T
          F~lat'
standardizedSolution(sem(compo3,data=dat))

Okay, if I have understood correctly 1 and 3 should be equivalent to 2. There are just two different ways of fixing the scale. Is this correct? But, why, when I fix the scale using 3 I get results equal to 2, something that makes more sense in the light of the relationship between the two variables of interest? Should I always fix the scale using the unstandardized parameter estimate without the minus sign, if this is negative?

Apologies for these simple questions, but I am a bit lost! Is there any comprehensive book dealing with these issues? I have searched for one, but no book seems to deal with this in an exhaustive manner.

thanks in advance!

Simone

messages.subject_clean: Saving ID Variable along predict()ed values
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I am currently struggling a bit with predict()ing latent factor scores from a fitted lavaan-model. I know that these are not "real" factor scores and that predicting them is not generally recommended, but let's just say I need to do it.

The model fitting and predict()ing actually works fine, except that lavaan removes 3,000 participants with no data at all out of 12,000 available. The problem is that I can't figure out which exact participants are excluded (na.omit() on the original data doesn't reproduce the N used by lavaan). As a consequence, I cannot attach the predicted values to the original data frame. Thus, I have two related questions:

1. Is it possible to figure out which individuals were excluded? lavaan warns me that some had no data but the output is truncated because of the sheer mass.

2. Is it possible to provide predict() with an id-variable so that this id is saved along the predicted values?

All the best,

Marcus

messages.subject: Re: Saving ID Variable along predict()ed values
messages.subject_clean: Saving ID Variable along predict()ed values
messages.body_plain:
Here is a dirty trick that you may use for matching the id variable. I just simply make a new model that includes the id variable and all observed variables used in the original model.

newdata <- HolzingerSwineford1939

newdata[seq(1, 301, 3), -1] <- NA

mod1 <- 'f1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3'

fit1 <- cfa(mod1, newdata)

pred1 <- predict(fit1)

mod2 <- 'id ~~ x1 + x2 + x3

'

fit2 <- cfa(mod2, newdata)

dat2 <- fit2@Data@X[[1]]

pred1 <- data.frame(pred1, id = dat2[,1])

messages.body_plain:
This could be a matter of scale differences between X and Y.  With a single predictor, a regression coefficient is essentially:

b = correlation(Y,X) * sd(Y)/sd(X)

If X has a very large variance and Y has a very small variance, then the ratio will be near zero, and so will b, regardless of the correlation.

If the result troubles you, take a look at the standardized estimate of the regression slope.

--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
Would it help to do this, versus just putting the 4 components of y into the second equation directly?  Lavaan estimates factor-based models, so it must obey factor-based rules.  Under those rules, there is no way for the algorithm to decide the weights for the four components of y.

     You could perhaps derive the numbers that you want using a sheaf coefficient:

http://intersci.ss.uci.edu/wiki/pdf/Heise1972NominalInducedandBlockvarsinregressionanal.pdf

The idea is that you allow the components to have direct effects on the ultimate dependent and then transform their combined contribution into an estimate of the coefficient for the composite predicting the dependent.  I think it is elegant and under-used.

--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
If your predictors / components are highly correlated, you are going to see negative weights.  If you don’t like negative partialed weights, you could avoid them by estimating your sheaf coefficients using correlation weights rather than regression weights.  Correlation weights ignore collinearity among the components, so if all zero order correlations with the dependent variable are positive, then the weights will be positive as well.

http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11336-009-9127-y#page-1

     Besides avoiding negative weights, correlation weights have superior properties in out-of-sample prediction, except when sample sized is very high and the actual predictability of the dependent variable is quite high.

http://jeb.sagepub.com/content/29/3/317.short

--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
It is not entirely clear to me what steps you took.  If you wanted to derive a value for the formatively defined variable, then yes, you add up the components using the weights.  But you don’t add up the weights to get another parameter.  As Heise notes in his Step 2, you compute the variance of the formatively defined variable using the standard formula:

Variance of the sum =

     Sum of the variances

     + 2 times the sum of the covariances

     You need the variance of the formatively defined variable in order to get the sheaf coefficient.

--Ed Rigdon

     I am not quite sure that I understand your question.  It seems to me there are factor-based techniques like factor-based SEM and composite-based techniques like partial least squares (PLS) path modeling or generalized structured component analysis (GSCA).  You can't estimate models of composites in a factor-based technique and vice versa.  Theo Dijkstra has blurred the lines a bit with his recent innovations, starting with PLS results and then transforming to factor-Model results.
     If you literally meant "estimators," though, then the answer is yes.  You can use least squares methods for both factor models and composite models.  But you won't find one package that estimates both kinds of models.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject_clean: How to integrate a Rasch measure into a SEM?
messages.body_plain:
On 08/10/2014 03:35 PM, Tobias Ludwig wrote:
> Thanks, sure, but the Rasch-model gives me a variance for every case. Is
> there a chance to specify this column in the model?

No. You have two options:

1) you retrieve the original dichotomous scores, and you just define
your exLV as a latent variable measured by these binary items

(and if you must be 'Rasch', you should also constrain the factor
loadings to be equal, by giving them the same label)

2) like Terry suggested, you specify a single-indicator latent variable,
and you specify the (residual) variance of the single variable to a
constant, defined as

(1 - rho) * var(x)

and 'rho' is a measure of reliability, which you can retrieve from the
RUMM output, and var(x) is the observed variance of the rash scores.

Yves.

5. Then in the regression for the dependent variable:' x9 ~ y1 + x8' I added the st. reg. coeff. I found in "1." to get 'x9 ~ y1 + 0.59*x8'

messages.subject: RE: Saving ID Variable along predict()ed values
messages.subject_clean: Saving ID Variable along predict()ed values
messages.body_plain:
Hans—

     Factor indeterminacy means that the common factor includes two parts: (1) a weighted function of all observed variables in the model, and (2) an arbitrary vector—call it S.  The pseudo factor scores that programs, including lavaan, give you are just the first part, omitting S.  So the fundamental problem with using these scores to represent a common factor is that they are not equal to the common factor.  So having gone to all this trouble, you have failed to achieve your objective.

     Note that S is “arbitrary,” not “random.”  If S were “random,” as in “random measurement error,” then you could easily adjust results from using pseudo factor scores to the results that you would have obtained from using actual factor scores.  And you would know that the correlation between pseudo factor scores and some outside variable would overstate the correlation between the factor and the outside variable, by a degree based on the extent of indeterminacy.  In other words, you could fix the problem.

     But S is “arbitrary.”  The only rule for S is that the S for each common factor must be orthogonal to every other S and orthogonal to every observed variable in the factor model.  Now, take your external variable, that you want to predict using these pseudo factor scores.  That variable is NOT in the factor model.  So we could construct an S using that criterion variable itself as our raw material.  First, we predict your criterion using the observed variables.  Then we take the residual, adjust it to get the proper variance, and we call that S.  Using that S would mean that the factor would have a HIGHER correlation with the criterion variable.  Or we multiply that by -1, and use that as S.  In this case, the factor could have a substantially LOWER correlation with the criterion.

     Let me emphasize that, if we construct S correctly, then both of these sets of actual factor scores would be perfectly consistent with the factor model.  They would BOTH be correct, in every way.  This uncertainty is the price of specifying factor models with a substantial degree of indeterminacy.  Researchers could keep indeterminacy low by specifying models with many strong indicators per common factor.  But that would magnify statistical power, leading to poor fit statistics, and it would increase the cost of data collection.

--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject_clean: Moderated path analysis???
messages.body_plain:
>
> I want to test the moderator path analysis.
> Could I directly use the product of moderator and X? Or do I need center the mean of X and moderator and then to get the product?
>
> My path model is following:
> model_id_moderator <- '
>      #regression
>      Z ~ Y1 + Y2 + Y3
>      Y1 ~ X1 + X1*Moderator
>      Y2 ~ X1 + X2
>      Y3 ~ X2 + X3
>      #correlation
>      Y1 ~~ Y2 + Y3
>      Y2 ~~ Y3
> '
>

Centering X1 and Moderator at their means only sometimes has the convenient result of lowering the correlation between the product term and each of the mean-centered variables.  Regardless, you will have to calculate the product term manually so it is included in your data.frame, then use the name of that product-term variable in your syntax.  For example,

dat$X1_Moderator <- dat$X1 * dat$Moderator

So you could simply calculate the product term from raw variables and again from mean-centered variables, then look at the correlation matrix among the product variables and the raw and mean-centered X1 and Moderator to see whether it even makes a noticeable difference.

Also, in your syntax, make sure to include all lower-order terms if they are involved in interactions.  Your current syntax constrains the effect of Moderator to be zero when X1 == 0 (i.e., change the line "Y1 ~ X1 + X1*Moderator" to "Y1 ~ X1 + Moderator + X1_Moderator").

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Hans—

     Yes, it makes a great deal of sense to include the criterion variable in the original factor model, rather than define the factor in one model and predict in another.

     You can easily calculate factor indeterminacy using model parameter values.  By varying those terms, you can see how changes affect the result.  I favor Louis Guttman’s (1955) index.  Guttman’s rho is equal to the minimal correlation between two different sets of factor scores for the same common factor.  This index ranges from -1 to +1, and is calculated as:

Guttman’s rho = [2 x R2(F,Y)] - 1

where R2(F,Y) is R square for the common factor when predicted by the observed variables.  R2(F,Y) is the “determinacy” number given by most SEM packages.

You can also calculate R2(F,Y) yourself as:

Diag(P x t(L) x inv(Sigma) x L x P)

Where:

P is factor covariance matrix

L is the loading matrix

Sigma is the observed variable covariance matrix

Diag means diagonal elements

t() means transpose

inv() means inverse

You will also find that Guttman’s rho tracks closely with composite reliability, especially for models with just one factor.  Indicators per factor, number of factors, strength of loadings and strength of factor correlations all affect rho, to some extent.

     How much indeterminacy can you stand?  The field is far from acknowledging the need to worry about this question.  If you took 0.80 (a common default minimum for statistical power), then in a model with, say several correlated factors, you might achieve rho = +0.80 with 3 indicators per factor with standardized loadings all at 0.90.  If standardized loadings are only 0.80, you will need 6 indicators per common factor.  Eitehr way, that’s more than you are going to see in the typical published application.

--Ed Rigdon

Guttman, L. (1955). The determinacy of factor score matrices with implications for five other basic problems of common-factor theory. The British Journal of Statistical Psychology, 8, 65-81.

messages.subject: Re: interpretation of partial measurement invariance
messages.subject_clean: interpretation of partial measurement invariance
messages.body_plain:
> So my question; is it okay to assume that I can pool the data of the groups and that I can compare the latent means when I reach partial metric and scalar invariance?

These are 2 questions.  As Steenkamp et al. (1998) discuss, the answer to your second question is "yes."  But your first questions confuses me.  By "pool the data of the groups" do you mean that you fit a single-group model to all data (i.e., from both groups, but ignoring the grouping variable)?  I believe the only time that is justified is when all parameters (factor loadings, intercepts, residual variances, latent variances/covariances/means) can be constrained to equality across groups.  Also, if you ignore grouping, then you can't compare group latent-means.  If you mean to fit a single-group model to all data and include a group-indicator variable (e.g., dummy code) to predict the latent mean, that model assumes that residual variances are equal across groups.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm currently running some measurement invariance tests, and have run into a small roadblock.  The authors I am working with are interested in a second-order/hierarchical model, which fits relatively well (using cfa(), and the options: std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, std.ov = TRUE, and orthogonal = TRUE).  This model has one overarching factor, and four sub-factors which load onto the items (each item only loads on one subfactor).

We are currently testing for invariance across gender, with the following syntax: measurementInvariance(model = model, data = data, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, std.ov = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE, group = "sex").

This approach works with the correlated CFA model (no overarching factor, without the orthogonal parameter), but when we apply it to the second-order factor, lavaan yields the following warning:

In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING: could not compute standard errors!

I thought this might be because a particular model might not have converged, but I reran the model with verbose = TRUE, and it appears each of the four models converged.  Is this function perhaps not designed for second-order CFAs?  Or am I doing something else wrong?

Any advice would be extremely appreciated!

Best,

Matt

messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure I follow the logic of what you are doing, but you say you have been able to do it in Mplus by saving parameter estimates as starting values with the SVALUE command (presumably changing each asterisk * to @ so they become constraints instead of starting values).  If this is the only thing you need to know how to do, then something like the following should work (although you should check the "C.syntax" to make sure it contains all the constraints you expect):

example(sem) ## just to get an example to work with
E.coefs <- parameterEstimates(fit)
E.coefs
C.syntax <- paste0(E.coefs$lhs, E.coefs$op, E.coefs$est, "*", E.coefs$rhs, collapse = "\n")
cat(C.syntax) ## this should be the syntax of constraints you need

There might be something easier or more clever that I am unaware of.

Terry

messages.subject_clean: Saving ID Variable along predict()ed values
messages.body_plain:
Dear Edward Ridgon,

Thank you for your elaborated comments.
I noticed myself that the correlations between predicted variables ("biased factor scores" for several variables) are not of equal in size to the correlations between the same variables when they are part of the same SEM model. And I think you delivered the explanation for this phenomenon. I am wondering though why SEM software like lavaan does not base their predict function on both the weighted function of observed variables and S. It would be really handy to get predicted factor scores that estimate the standing of people on the latent trait of interest especially because including many latent traits and external criteria into SEM models often causes computational difficulties.

best,
Michael

On Monday, August 18, 2014 8:29:04 PM UTC+2, Edward Rigdon wrote:
>
> Hans—
>
>      Factor indeterminacy means that the common factor includes two parts: (1) a weighted function of all observed variables in the model, and (2) an arbitrary vector—call it S.  The pseudo factor scores that programs, including lavaan, give you are just the first part, omitting S.  So the fundamental problem with using these scores to represent a common factor is that they are not equal to the common factor.  So having gone to all this trouble, you have failed to achieve your objective.
>
>      Note that S is “arbitrary,” not “random.”  If S were “random,” as in “random measurement error,” then you could easily adjust results from using pseudo factor scores to the results that you would have obtained from using actual factor scores.  And you would know that the correlation between pseudo factor scores and some outside variable would overstate the correlation between the factor and the outside variable, by a degree based on the extent of indeterminacy.  In other words, you could fix the problem.
>
>      But S is “arbitrary.”  The only rule for S is that the S for each common factor must be orthogonal to every other S and orthogonal to every observed variable in the factor model.  Now, take your external variable, that you want to predict using these pseudo factor scores.  That variable is NOT in the factor model.  So we could construct an S using that criterion variable itself as our raw material.  First, we predict your criterion using the observed variables.  Then we take the residual, adjust it to get the proper variance, and we call that S.  Using that S would mean that the factor would have a HIGHER correlation with the criterion variable.  Or we multiply that by -1, and use that as S.  In this case, the factor could have a substantially LOWER correlation with the criterion.
>
>      Let me emphasize that, if we construct S correctly, then both of these sets of actual factor scores would be perfectly consistent with the factor model.  They would BOTH be correct, in every way.  This uncertainty is the price of specifying factor models with a substantial degree of indeterminacy.  Researchers could keep indeterminacy low by specifying models with many strong indicators per common factor.  But that would magnify statistical power, leading to poor fit statistics, and it would increase the cost of data collection.
>
> --Ed Rigdon
>

messages.subject: Re: Saving ID Variable along predict()ed values
messages.subject_clean: Saving ID Variable along predict()ed values
messages.body_plain:
Michael--
     Remember that each S is arbitrary.  Where factors are indeterminate, there is no one answer.  Any one set of actual factor scores is just one of the infinity of possible sets, none of them any more correct than any of the others.  It is not hard to create your own S for each common factor, if that males things better.
    This limitation of the factor model would not seem so strange if the literature had not spent decades suppressing this topic--telling users that "fit" is all they needed, which in turn leads users to specify factor models with higher indeterminacy.  You can minimize the indeterminacy problem by specifying factor models with more and better indicators, though that makes it even more challenging to obtain good fit. Factor models with few and only moderately strong indicators per factor, which are more likely to pass fit tests, are going to have substantial indeterminacy.  There is no free lunch.

--Ed Rigdon

Sent from my iPad

Yves,

A user recently brought something to my attention that causes a problem with the nesting/equivalence testing function in semTools.  When using WLS estimator, net() returns an error that if the raw data is not provided, the WLS.V weight matrix must be provided along with the sample.cov/means/nobs.  But when I pass the WLS.V matrix, I still get an error that seems to regard the thresholds (which I don't think can be passed to the lavaan function like WLS.V can).

Could you suggest a solution, or let me know whether the net() help page should warn that the implementation does not work for WLS?  I provide example syntax below to reproduce the error that I can't figure a way to solve.  Thank you,

Terry

> library(lavaan)
>
> myData <- read.table("http://www.statmodel.com/usersguide/chap5/ex5.16.dat")
> names(myData) <- c("u1","u2","u3","u4","u5","u6","x1","x2","x3","g")
>

> ## specify less restricted model
> mod1 <- '
> f1 =~ u1 + u2 + u3
> f2 =~ u4 + u5 + u6
> '
> ## fit both models to data

> fit1 <- cfa(mod1, data = myData, ordered = paste0("u", 1:6))

>

> myFit <- lavaan(sample.cov = R, sample.mean = M, sample.nobs = nrow(myData),

messages.subject: Re: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite
messages.subject_clean: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite
messages.body_plain:
Dear Yves Rosseel,

You mentioned that we can ignore the warning if the negative value of the last eigenvalue is really tiny.
The last eigenvalue of my covariance matrix is negative:
> eigen(inspect(NARQ.NPI.fit, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>"))$values
 [1]  1.48731263  0.64165345  0.42265603  0.39206208  0.21803107  0.17784040  0.14245618  0.05661914  0.03808006 -0.0770958

I think the reason why I have this negative eigenvalue is that I have constructs in my model that are highly positively correlated. However, I would like to keep both constructs separately in my model because I want to see to what degree two personality instruments measure the same latent traits. I would like to see how strongly the latent traits of the two personality instruments correlate.
So, I would be happy to ignore the warning and interpret the summary of the output that I got.
However, I know that if the last eigenvalue is zero or negative, the determinant will be 0 or negative as well and the determinant might be used for some computations by lavaan. So, just to be on the safe side, I wonder: Does lavaan use the determinant for further computations? and is a negative eigenvalue and determinant then problematic?
My ultimate question is: can I rely on the output of the CFA even though the last eigenvalue is negative (-0.0770958)?

> Perhaps I should clarify the meaning of positive definite. A symmetric

>
> eigen( inspect(modelcfa3.1, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") )$values
>
> If the negative value is really, really tiny, it is probably safe, and
> you can ignore the warning.
>
> But judging from your factor correlations, it looks like the two latent
> variables 'Analytical_Thinking' and 'Planning_Organising' (corr = 0.978)
> are almost identical. I would remove one of the two, or rethink the
> measurement model (ie the indicators) for these two latent variables.
>
> Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Ed Ridgon,

Thanks for the response.

Ok, so, because the S for a latent trait is arbitrary and there is no one answer, I am asking myself: how does SEM software like lavaan determine the S for a latent trait in the SEM model?
Does lavaan pick a S that increases the correlation between the variables (latent traits) in the SEM model? (in this case, other variables in the model would serve as additional indicators)
But you said that the rule for S is that it is orthogonal to any other S in the model and orthogonal to any observed variable in the model. So, I guess this rule is in place to make sure that the correlations between variables in the SEM model do not get under- or overestimated. Is that the reason why we should have both variables in the model?

Do you think it is ok to use the predicted factor scores when there are many decent indicators in the model on which the predictions are based (because then the degree of indeterminacy would be low). So, do you think it would be ok to use the "pseudo factor scores" when I have say 10 indicators with standardized loadings of .5 on average?
On the other hand, if we have only few or weak indicators of a construct, then it would be better to compute correlations/regressions etc. within the SEM model instead relying on the "pseudo factor scores", right?

A potentially related question: Could it be that the S of the latent trait A also influences the factor loadings of the indicators (items) of A. In my experience, an items factor loading on the latent trait A is slightly different in a SEM model with only the latent trait A in the model compared to a SEM model in which there is not only A with the indicators of A but also a second latent trait B and the indicators of B in the SEM model (at least that's the case when A and B are correlated). Why are the factor loadings on one factor not independent of the presence or absence of another factor and its indicators in the SEM model? could the orthogonality of the S of A and the S of B be the reason?

Michael

messages.body_plain:
Factor models are great for estimating factor model parameters.  Think of a factor model as a pocket universe with its own set of rules.  Indeterminacy becomes an issue when you try to go outside the model.  That is a contrast with composite-based models, where a weighted sum is a weighted sum is a weighted sum.  If you want to use a common factor as a predictor, you should include the dependent variable within the factor model.
     Loadings of 0.5 are small.  Ten indicators would not be enough.  Everything is a matter of degree, but there is certainly some point where indeterminacy is small enough to be ignored.
     Introducing another common factor, or even just more indicators, can certainly change factor model outcomes.  A model is only fit within the given set of conditions.  Whenever new variables are included in a model, the "best" solution can certainly change.   Evidence from a factor model is conditional on the model.

--Ed Rigdon

Sent from my iPad

On Aug 26, 2014, at 7:13 AM, Michael Paul Grosz <michael.p...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Ed Ridgon,
>
> Thanks for the response.
>
> Ok, so, because the S for a latent trait is arbitrary and there is no one answer, I am asking myself: how does SEM software like lavaan determine the S for a latent trait in the SEM model?
> Does lavaan pick a S that increases the correlation between the variables (latent traits) in the SEM model? (in this case, other variables in the model would serve as additional indicators)
> But you said that the rule for S is that it is orthogonal to any other S in the model and orthogonal to any observed variable in the model. So, I guess this rule is in place to make sure that the correlations between variables in the SEM model do not get under- or overestimated. Is that the reason why we should have both variables in the model?
>
> Do you think it is ok to use the predicted factor scores when there are many decent indicators in the model on which the predictions are based (because then the degree of indeterminacy would be low). So, do you think it would be ok to use the "pseudo factor scores" when I have say 10 indicators with standardized loadings of .5 on average?
> On the other hand, if we have only few or weak indicators of a construct, then it would be better to compute correlations/regressions etc. within the SEM model instead relying on the "pseudo factor scores", right?
>
> A potentially related question: Could it be that the S of the latent trait A also influences the factor loadings of the indicators (items) of A. In my experience, an items factor loading on the latent trait A is slightly different in a SEM model with only the latent trait A in the model compared to a SEM model in which there is not only A with the indicators of A but also a second latent trait B and the indicators of B in the SEM model (at least that's the case when A and B are correlated). Why are the factor loadings on one factor not independent of the presence or absence of another factor and its indicators in the SEM model? could the orthogonality of the S of A and the S of B be the reason?
>
> Michael
>
> On Tuesday, August 26, 2014 12:24:32 AM UTC+2, Edward Rigdon wrote:
> > Michael--
> >      Remember that each S is arbitrary.  Where factors are indeterminate, there is no one answer.  Any one set of actual factor scores is just one of the infinity of possible sets, none of them any more correct than any of the others.  It is not hard to create your own S for each common factor, if that males things better.
> >     This limitation of the factor model would not seem so strange if the literature had not spent decades suppressing this topic--telling users that "fit" is all they needed, which in turn leads users to specify factor models with higher indeterminacy.  You can minimize the indeterminacy problem by specifying factor models with more and better indicators, though that makes it even more challenging to obtain good fit. Factor models with few and only moderately strong indicators per factor, which are more likely to pass fit tests, are going to have substantial indeterminacy.  There is no free lunch.
> > --Ed Rigdon
> >
> > Sent from my iPad
> >
> > On Aug 25, 2014, at 3:51 PM, Michael Paul Grosz <michael.p...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > Dear Edward Ridgon,
> > >
> > > Thank you for your elaborated comments.
> > > I noticed myself that the correlations between predicted variables ("biased factor scores" for several variables) are not of equal in size to the correlations between the same variables when they are part of the same SEM model. And I think you delivered the explanation for this phenomenon. I am wondering though why SEM software like lavaan does not base their predict function on both the weighted function of observed variables and S. It would be really handy to get predicted factor scores that estimate the standing of people on the latent trait of interest especially because including many latent traits and external criteria into SEM models often causes computational difficulties.
> > >
> > > best,
> > > Michael
> > >
> > > On Monday, August 18, 2014 8:29:04 PM UTC+2, Edward Rigdon wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hans—
> > > >
> > > >      Factor indeterminacy means that the common factor includes two parts: (1) a weighted function of all observed variables in the model, and (2) an arbitrary vector—call it S.  The pseudo factor scores that programs, including lavaan, give you are just the first part, omitting S.  So the fundamental problem with using these scores to represent a common factor is that they are not equal to the common factor.  So having gone to all this trouble, you have failed to achieve your objective.
> > > >
> > > >      Note that S is “arbitrary,” not “random.”  If S were “random,” as in “random measurement error,” then you could easily adjust results from using pseudo factor scores to the results that you would have obtained from using actual factor scores.  And you would know that the correlation between pseudo factor scores and some outside variable would overstate the correlation between the factor and the outside variable, by a degree based on the extent of indeterminacy.  In other words, you could fix the problem.
> > > >
> > > >      But S is “arbitrary.”  The only rule for S is that the S for each common factor must be orthogonal to every other S and orthogonal to every observed variable in the factor model.  Now, take your external variable, that you want to predict using these pseudo factor scores.  That variable is NOT in the factor model.  So we could construct an S using that criterion variable itself as our raw material.  First, we predict your criterion using the observed variables.  Then we take the residual, adjust it to get the proper variance, and we call that S.  Using that S would mean that the factor would have a HIGHER correlation with the criterion variable.  Or we multiply that by -1, and use that as S.  In this case, the factor could have a substantially LOWER correlation with the criterion.
> > > >
> > > >      Let me emphasize that, if we construct S correctly, then both of these sets of actual factor scores would be perfectly consistent with the factor model.  They would BOTH be correct, in every way.  This uncertainty is the price of specifying factor models with a substantial degree of indeterminacy.  Researchers could keep indeterminacy low by specifying models with many strong indicators per common factor.  But that would magnify statistical power, leading to poor fit statistics, and it would increase the cost of data collection.
> > > >
> > > > --Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
The un standardized parameter estimates and standard errors for age squared are small partly because the variance of age squared is so large, relative to that of the dependent variable.  (The standard errors are not 0, but they are scaled a few decimal places to the left.)  If you have a doubt, run the model without the squared terms, and compare the R2 for the factors from that model with the R2 here.  The increment in R2 will tell you if the squared term is making a practically significant contribution.
--Ed Rigdon

Why are the factor loadings on one factor not independent of the presence or absence of another factor and its indicators in the SEM model? could the orthogonality of the S of A and the S of B be the reason?
> >
> > Michael
> >
> > On Tuesday, August 26, 2014 12:24:32 AM UTC+2, Edward Rigdon wrote:
> > > Michael--
> > >      Remember that each S is arbitrary.  Where factors are indeterminate, there is no one answer.  Any one set of actual factor scores is just one of the infinity of possible sets, none of them any more correct than any of the others.  It is not hard to create your own S for each common factor, if that males things better.
> > >     This limitation of the factor model would not seem so strange if the literature had not spent decades suppressing this topic--telling users that "fit" is all they needed, which in turn leads users to specify factor models with higher indeterminacy.  You can minimize the indeterminacy problem by specifying factor models with more and better indicators, though that makes it even more challenging to obtain good fit. Factor models with few and only moderately strong indicators per factor, which are more likely to pass fit tests, are going to have substantial indeterminacy.  There is no free lunch.
> > > --Ed Rigdon
> > >
> > > Sent from my iPad
> > >
> > > On Aug 25, 2014, at 3:51 PM, Michael Paul Grosz <michael.p...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > Dear Edward Ridgon,
> > > >
> > > > Thank you for your elaborated comments.
> > > > I noticed myself that the correlations between predicted variables ("biased factor scores" for several variables) are not of equal in size to the correlations between the same variables when they are part of the same SEM model. And I think you delivered the explanation for this phenomenon. I am wondering though why SEM software like lavaan does not base their predict function on both the weighted function of observed variables and S. It would be really handy to get predicted factor scores that estimate the standing of people on the latent trait of interest especially because including many latent traits and external criteria into SEM models often causes computational difficulties.
> > > >
> > > > best,
> > > > Michael
> > > >
> > > > On Monday, August 18, 2014 8:29:04 PM UTC+2, Edward Rigdon wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > Hans—
> > > > >
> > > > >      Factor indeterminacy means that the common factor includes two parts: (1) a weighted function of all observed variables in the model, and (2) an arbitrary vector—call it S.  The pseudo factor scores that programs, including lavaan, give you are just the first part, omitting S.  So the fundamental problem with using these scores to represent a common factor is that they are not equal to the common factor.  So having gone to all this trouble, you have failed to achieve your objective.
> > > > >
> > > > >      Note that S is “arbitrary,” not “random.”  If S were “random,” as in “random measurement error,” then you could easily adjust results from using pseudo factor scores to the results that you would have obtained from using actual factor scores.  And you would know that the correlation between pseudo factor scores and some outside variable would overstate the correlation between the factor and the outside variable, by a degree based on the extent of indeterminacy.  In other words, you could fix the problem.
> > > > >
> > > > >      But S is “arbitrary.”  The only rule for S is that the S for each common factor must be orthogonal to every other S and orthogonal to every observed variable in the factor model.  Now, take your external variable, that you want to predict using these pseudo factor scores.  That variable is NOT in the factor model.  So we could construct an S using that criterion variable itself as our raw material.  First, we predict your criterion using the observed variables.  Then we take the residual, adjust it to get the proper variance, and we call that S.  Using that S would mean that the factor would have a HIGHER correlation with the criterion variable.  Or we multiply that by -1, and use that as S.  In this case, the factor could have a substantially LOWER correlation with the criterion.
> > > > >
> > > > >      Let me emphasize that, if we construct S correctly, then both of these sets of actual factor scores would be perfectly consistent with the factor model.  They would BOTH be correct, in every way.  This uncertainty is the price of specifying factor models with a substantial degree of indeterminacy.  Researchers could keep indeterminacy low by specifying models with many strong indicators per common factor.  But that would magnify statistical power, leading to poor fit statistics, and it would increase the cost of data collection.

messages.subject_clean: group analysis error for missing category
messages.body_plain:
This seems like an interesting phenomenon, and is something I thought about a while back as well (I'm somewhat surprised to hear it exists in Mplus and LISREAL though). What happens when estimating intercept parameters in multiple group settings where one group has no instantiations of a relevant category is that no information about the parameter estimate can come from that respective group (e.g., when maximizing the likelihood, all the likelihood information comes from only one group instead of two). This isn't to say that it doesn't exist, it's just that it doesn't exist in isolation when considering one group at a time, and this can cause issues for estimators which need intercept and covariance parameters to be identified for each group. Basically, the idea is to set the parameter estimates equal across group so that they can be uniquely identified, but for the group without the category of interest the parameter is really just a placeholder since all the information comes from other sources. I've attached an example which doesn't require collapsing the data arbitrarily to get around this, and I imagine lavaan could do something like this as well (at least with the MML estimator, not sure about the others). Cheers.

Phil

I would recommend trying to preserve the nature of your test to the best of your ability, since in the end that's likely what you are trying to understand. messages.subject: Is it necessary to state the items are ordered when using the WLSMV estimator?
messages.subject_clean: Is it necessary to state the items are ordered when using the WLSMV estimator?
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I’m trying to perform a cfa of a psychological battery that has 37 items, for which prior cfa suggest has an 11 factor structure; each of the 37 items is rated on a 7-point Likert scale.

When this psychological battery was first published, cfa showed it had barely adequate fit measures, and subsequently the authors suggested that four pairs of items should have their error covariances freed to improve fit.

I thought I would free these covariances by adding terms like  x1 ~~ x2 to the model, because the modification indices in my data suggested that these same four pairs of residual covariances should be freed. However I was nervous about doing this because one of the four pairs of residual covariances was for items that were supposed to load onto different latent variables.

This model that had the four free residual covariances freed  had a better fit than the model that didn’t free them when I fit it to the entire sample.  But when I tested the measurement invariance in ethnic groups, I ran into problems, and I would like to ask your advice.  What I would like to ask is: do I have to state in the cfa() that the items are ordered if I am going to use estimator=”WLSMV”  ?

Because I misunderstood the code stating ordered=c(item1, item2, . .. . ), I didn’t include it when I started, and it seemed to work well, giving me no warnings.  However, I now realise that I should declare to lavaan that the data are ordinal, so I added it and removed the term estimator=”WLSMV”, but this gave me the warning:   “lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite; use inspect(fit,"cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") to investigate.”

When I inspected the covariance of latent variables, all were positive, but when I looked at the eigenvalues the last one was negative: 2.9701287206  0.8247727438  0.8082874014  0.4886781682  0.4381578907  0.3166371107  0.2648484386  0.1378354428  0.0781594220  0.0691967668 -0.0004707457

The eigenvalues were all positive when I didn’t include the ordered statement in the cfa():[1] 9.5142774 3.3008226 2.7263258 2.0661703 1.6764486 1.2925841 0.8536194 0.5164931 0.2943799 0.1629691 0.0453801

Is it vital to tell Lavaan that the items are ordinal before using the estimator WLSMV?

I think the cause of my problem is the freeing of the residual covariances of the four pairs of items, because in the model that does not free them, I get no warnings when I fit it with the statement that the items are ordered in the cfa() code, and the eigenvalues are all positive [1] 3.00074635 0.86855023 0.82474092 0.49010797 0.43912718 0.31956604 0.27525692 0.22408847 0.10381235 0.07781825 0.02671555

What do you think? Can I use estimator=”WLSMV” without specifying the data are ordinal, or does the fact that lavaan gives me a warning message and the last eigenvalue is negative, suggest that it was wrong to free the residual errors of the four pairs of items?  Could the reason I am having problems when I look at the fit in subsamples simply be because the size of the subsamples is too small to account for the amount of covariance?

Thank you so much for your help.

Best wishes

Brent

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ross,

I have not been able to get Lavaan to fit my model on my second sample, using the parameter estimated from the first sample as fixed parameters. Lavaan would treat it as starting values.
If somebody knows why, I would also appreciate to find out why. In Mplus, using the Svalue option in output, your are given the full model command which you just need to copy and paste.

I am not expert in Cross Validation but as far as I understand, you are supposed to predict the values of the manifest variables in the test sample from the model given by the training sample.
This means that you need to use the parameter estimates of the training sample (loadings, variances, covariances and means of the manifest variables) on the data of the test sample.
For this, you will need the factor scores (which is given by predict in Lavaan and by Save=fscores in Mplus).
One thing unclear to me is should one use the factor scores predicted by the training sample or by the test sample ?
I would personally choose the factor scores predicted by the test sample because otherwise where would I use the test sample data...?

In any case, I believe that by fixing the parameters, your degree of freedom changes. Used on the same sample, the fit should remain the same (as per the residual matrix and the most of the fit indices.
Used on the other half of the sample, the degree of misfit should give you an indication of the stability of your model.

I hope that helps...

Franck
